conflicts/first-crusade/name: The First Crusade and the Rhineland massacres
conflicts/first-crusade/religionRoleNote: Religion was the main stated and, most historians now agree, the main real motive. Urban II offered remission of the penance due for sin to those who went to free the Eastern churches and Jerusalem 'for devotion alone, not to gain honour or money'. Older interpretations stressed land-hungry younger sons and economic pressures; Jonathan Riley-Smith and others showed from charters that crusaders sold or mortgaged property at great cost and were often eldest sons and established lords, motivated by penitential piety, pilgrimage and the reform movement. Other factors still mattered: the Byzantine appeal for help, papal ambitions after the schism of 1054 and the Investiture Controversy, the ambitions of princes such as Bohemond and Baldwin, and the lure of booty once on campaign. On the Muslim side the Seljuk and Fatimid rulers were initially slow to treat the invasion as a religious war.
conflicts/first-crusade/sides/0/leaders/: Raymond of Saint-Gilles, count of Toulouse
conflicts/first-crusade/sides/2/name: Seljuk Turks and Syrian Muslim rulers
conflicts/first-crusade/sides/4/leaders/: Communal leaders of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, such as Kalonymus ben Meshullam of Mainz
conflicts/first-crusade/summary: Responding to a Byzantine appeal for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II at Clermont in November 1095 called on Western knights to liberate the Eastern Christians and Jerusalem in return for remission of sins. Tens of thousands took the cross. Popular bands massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096; the main armies took Nicaea, survived the terrible siege of Antioch and captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing much of its Muslim and Jewish population. The crusade created the Latin states of the East and the enduring institution of crusading.
conflicts/first-crusade/story:
In the eleventh century the Seljuk Turks had taken most of Anatolia from the Byzantine Empire after the battle of Manzikert (1071) and had seized Jerusalem from the Fatimids in 1073 (the Fatimids retook it in 1098). Western pilgrims reported difficulties on the road to the Holy Sepulchre, which had been destroyed by the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim in 1009 and later rebuilt. In March 1095 envoys of the emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza for military help. Urban, a reforming pope who had been driven from Rome during the Investiture Controversy, saw an opportunity to direct the violence of the knightly class towards a holy purpose, to aid the Eastern Church after the breach of 1054 and to assert papal leadership.

On 27 November 1095, at the end of the Council of Clermont, Urban preached in a field outside the town. No verbatim text survives; later accounts by Fulcher of Chartres, Robert the Monk and others differ, but agree that he described the sufferings of Eastern Christians and the pollution of the holy places, and offered that the journey would count for all penance. The crowd is said to have cried 'Deus vult!' (God wills it), and many sewed cloth crosses onto their garments. Urban toured France preaching, and popular preachers such as Peter the Hermit spread the message more widely than the pope intended.

In spring 1096 popular bands set out before the princes. Some, led by Count Emicho of Flonheim and others, turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland, arguing that it was wrong to march against God's enemies far away while leaving 'the killers of Christ' at home, and seeking money. At Speyer in early May the bishop protected most of the Jews; at Worms in mid-May some 800 were killed, including those sheltering in the bishop's palace; at Mainz on 27 May the archbishop's protection collapsed and the community was destroyed, many choosing to kill their families and themselves rather than be baptised. Killings and forced baptisms followed at Cologne, Trier, Metz, Regensburg and Prague. Hebrew chronicles such as that of Solomon bar Samson remember these as the martyrdoms of 1096. Peter the Hermit's army reached Constantinople and crossed into Asia, where the Turks destroyed it at Civetot in October 1096; Emicho's band was dispersed in Hungary.

The princely armies converged on Constantinople over the winter of 1096–1097, where most leaders swore to return former imperial lands to Alexios. Together with Byzantine forces they besieged Nicaea, which surrendered to the Byzantines on 19 June 1097, and defeated Kilij Arslan at Dorylaeum on 1 July. After a gruelling march across Anatolia, Baldwin of Boulogne broke away to take Edessa, founding the first crusader state in 1098. The main army besieged Antioch from October 1097; starvation and desertion were severe. On 3 June 1098 Bohemond secured the city through a traitor in a tower, and the crusaders massacred much of the population. Days later they were themselves besieged by the relief army of Kerbogha of Mosul. The 'discovery' of the Holy Lance by the visionary Peter Bartholomew revived morale, and on 28 June the crusaders defeated Kerbogha outside the walls. Adhemar of Le Puy died in August, and quarrels between Bohemond and Raymond delayed the march. At Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in December 1098 the crusaders massacred the inhabitants, and chroniclers including Radulph of Caen and Albert of Aachen record that starving soldiers ate the flesh of the dead.

The army, perhaps reduced to some 12,000–15,000 fighting men, reached Jerusalem, now held by the Fatimids, on 7 June 1099. After a failed assault, a barefoot penitential procession round the walls and the arrival of Genoese timber for siege towers, Godfrey of Bouillon's men broke in on 15 July. The crusaders killed large numbers of the Muslim inhabitants, including people who had taken refuge on the Temple Mount (the Haram al-Sharif), and burned the city's main synagogue with Jews inside, according to Muslim sources; others were ransomed, as letters in the Cairo Geniza show. Latin writers boasted that men waded in blood; Muslim writers later gave figures of 70,000 or more, which modern historians such as Benjamin Kedar regard as greatly inflated, with a toll of perhaps around 3,000 suggested by the near-contemporary Ibn al-Arabi. Godfrey became ruler with the title 'advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.

On 12 August 1099 the crusaders defeated a Fatimid relief army at Ascalon, and most survivors went home. Four Latin states, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, the Kingdom of Jerusalem and later the County of Tripoli, were established. The success was taken in the West as a miracle confirming that God willed the crusade; it inspired further expeditions and the creation of the military orders, but it also embittered relations with Byzantium, which had expected the return of Antioch, and in time provoked a Muslim counter-crusade.
conflicts/first-crusade/nameOfGod: Urban II framed the expedition as an armed pilgrimage and act of penance: those who went for devotion alone would have the journey counted in place of all penance for confessed sins. Participants took vows and wore the cross, recalling Christ's command to 'take up his cross' (Matthew 16:24), and the cry 'Deus vult!' became the crusaders' slogan. Clergy accompanied the armies, fasts, processions and visions (the Holy Lance at Antioch, appearances of warrior saints such as St George) punctuated the campaign, and the dead were spoken of as martyrs. The Rhineland attackers justified killing Jews as vengeance for the crucifixion, contrary to the teaching of popes and bishops that Jews should not be harmed.
conflicts/first-crusade/religiousCauses/: The papacy's call to liberate Eastern Christians and the Holy Sepulchre, and its offer of remission of penance to participants.
A penitential piety among the knightly class, shaped by the Gregorian reform, the Peace and Truce of God and the tradition of pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
Reports of the sufferings of Eastern Christians and pilgrims, and memory of al-Hakim's destruction of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009.
Apocalyptic expectations attached to Jerusalem among popular preachers and crusaders.
Anti-Jewish ideas of collective guilt for the crucifixion, which fuelled the Rhineland massacres.
conflicts/first-crusade/otherCauses/0: Alexios I's need for Western mercenaries to recover Anatolia after Manzikert (1071).
conflicts/first-crusade/otherCauses/1: Papal ambitions to lead Christendom during the Investiture Controversy and to heal the breach of 1054 with the Eastern Church.
conflicts/first-crusade/otherCauses/2: The ambitions of individual princes, such as Bohemond and Baldwin, for lordships in the East.
conflicts/first-crusade/otherCauses/3: Divisions among the Seljuk rulers after the death of Sultan Malik-Shah in 1092 and the Seljuk–Fatimid rivalry, which made the Muslim Near East vulnerable.
conflicts/first-crusade/otherCauses/4: Booty and the prospect of material reward once the campaign was underway.
conflicts/first-crusade/triggers/0: The appeal of Alexios I's envoys at the Council of Piacenza in March 1095.
conflicts/first-crusade/triggers/1: Urban II's sermon at Clermont on 27 November 1095.
conflicts/first-crusade/triggers/2: The preaching of Peter the Hermit and others, which launched the popular crusades and the attacks on Jews in spring 1096.
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/0/text: Seljuk victory at Manzikert opens Anatolia to the Turks.
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/1/text: Byzantine envoys at Piacenza (March); Urban II preaches the crusade at Clermont (27 November).
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/2/text: Rhineland massacres of Jews at Speyer, Worms, Mainz and elsewhere (May–June); People's Crusade destroyed at Civetot (October).
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/3/text: Princes' armies at Constantinople; Nicaea surrenders (19 June); victory at Dorylaeum (1 July); siege of Antioch begins (October).
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/4/text: Baldwin takes Edessa; Antioch falls (3 June); Kerbogha defeated (28 June); massacre at Ma'arrat al-Nu'man (December).
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/5/text: Siege of Jerusalem from 7 June; city stormed and massacre (15 July); victory at Ascalon (12 August).
conflicts/first-crusade/timeline/6/text: Death of Godfrey; Baldwin I becomes first king of Jerusalem.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/0/focu: Proclaimed the crusade at Clermont and organised its preaching and leadership.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/0/outc: Died on 29 July 1099, two weeks after Jerusalem fell, before the news reached him; beatified in 1881.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/1/focu: Raised and led the largest of the popular armies, destroyed at Civetot; later joined the main army.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/1/outc: Returned to Europe and founded a priory at Neufmoustier near Huy.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/2/role: Leader of a popular crusade band
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/2/focu: Led the massacres of Jews at Mainz and elsewhere in May 1096.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/2/outc: His army was defeated in Hungary; condemned by contemporary Christian and Jewish chroniclers.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/3/role: Bishop of Le Puy and papal legate
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/3/focu: Spiritual leader of the crusade, conciliating the princes and the Byzantines.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/3/outc: Died of disease at Antioch on 1 August 1098.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/4/focu: Led one of the main armies and was among the first to enter Jerusalem.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/4/outc: Ruled Jerusalem as 'advocate of the Holy Sepulchre' until his death in 1100; idealised in later legend.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/5/focu: Led the largest army, sponsored the Holy Lance and besieged Jerusalem from the south.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/5/outc: Began the conquest of the County of Tripoli and died besieging it.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/6/focu: Secured the capture of Antioch and kept it for himself despite oaths to Alexios.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/6/outc: Prince of Antioch; later led an unsuccessful war against Byzantium in 1107–1108.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/7/focu: Appealed for Western help, secured the princes' oaths and recovered Nicaea and western Anatolia.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/7/outc: Regained much of Anatolia but distrusted the Latins after Antioch; portrayed in his daughter Anna Komnene's Alexiad.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/8/focu: Destroyed the People's Crusade but lost Nicaea and the battle of Dorylaeum.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/8/outc: Moved his capital to Konya and continued to fight later crusades.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/9/focu: Expelled the city's Christians and defended Jerusalem in 1099.
conflicts/first-crusade/keyPeople/9/outc: Surrendered the Tower of David to Raymond and was allowed to leave for Ascalon with his garrison.
conflicts/first-crusade/casualties/note: No reliable overall figure exists. Modern estimates of those who set out range widely, perhaps 60,000–100,000 including non-combatants, and many more died of hunger and disease than in battle. The Rhineland massacres killed probably several thousand Jews; Hebrew sources name about 800 dead at Worms and over 1,000 at Mainz. For Jerusalem in 1099 Muslim figures of 70,000 or more are rejected by modern historians; Benjamin Kedar notes a near-contemporary estimate of about 3,000, while others think the toll was higher. Losses at Antioch and Ma'arra were also heavy but cannot be counted.
conflicts/first-crusade/effects/0: Four Latin states were established in Syria and Palestine, lasting in some form until 1291.
conflicts/first-crusade/effects/1: Jewish communities of the Rhineland were devastated, beginning a long pattern of crusade-related violence against European Jews.
conflicts/first-crusade/effects/2: Relations between Latin Christians and Byzantium were strained by disputes over Antioch and mutual distrust.
conflicts/first-crusade/effects/3: Muslim rulers gradually developed a counter-crusade ideology of jihad, culminating under Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin.
conflicts/first-crusade/effects/4: Italian maritime cities (Genoa, Pisa, Venice) gained trading privileges in the eastern Mediterranean.
conflicts/first-crusade/effectsOnChurch/: Crusading became an enduring institution of the Latin Church, with vows, indulgences and papal direction, later applied to Spain, the Baltic and heretics.
Military religious orders (the Templars and Hospitallers) emerged in the crusader states.
Latin patriarchs were installed in Antioch and Jerusalem, displacing Greek hierarchs and deepening the East–West schism.
The papacy's prestige and claim to lead Christendom were greatly enhanced.
Eastern Christians under crusader rule (Syriac, Armenian, Greek) experienced both protection and subordination to Latin clergy.
conflicts/first-crusade/legacy: The First Crusade was remembered in the West as a miraculous triumph and became the model for later crusades and crusading rhetoric. In Jewish memory it is the trauma of 1096, commemorated in liturgical laments. In the Muslim world it was at first a marginal event and only later became a symbol of Western aggression, a theme revived in modern politics. Popes have since expressed regret for violence committed in the name of the faith, notably John Paul II during the Day of Pardon in 2000.
conflicts/first-crusade/dissenters/0/nam: Bishop John of Speyer and other Rhineland bishops
conflicts/first-crusade/dissenters/0/tex: In May 1096 Bishop John of Speyer protected the Jews of his city and punished attackers, and Archbishop Hermann III of Cologne hid Jews in surrounding villages, acting on the long-standing church teaching that Jews were not to be killed or forcibly baptised; the archbishop of Mainz tried but failed to protect his city's Jews.
conflicts/first-crusade/dissenters/1/tex: Anselm wrote to monks forbidding them to leave their cloisters to join the expedition, insisting that their true Jerusalem was the 'vision of peace' within the monastery.
conflicts/first-crusade/dissenters/2/tex: The Byzantine princess and historian expressed in the Alexiad her disapproval of Latin priests who took up arms and fought, contrasting this with Orthodox canon law forbidding clergy to shed blood, and her mistrust of the crusaders' motives.
conflicts/first-crusade/theatres/1/name: Massacre of the Jews of Worms
conflicts/first-crusade/theatres/2/name: Massacre of the Jews of Mainz
conflicts/first-crusade/theatres/3/name: Civetot, destruction of the People's Crusade
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/0/peop: The main crusade armies of Godfrey, Raymond, Bohemond, the two Roberts and others
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/0/text: The armies travelled by separate routes to Constantinople, then together took Nicaea, fought at Dorylaeum, crossed Anatolia via Heraclea and Marash, besieged Antioch for eight months, marched south past Ma'arra and down the Lebanese coast to Jerusalem.
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/1/peop: Peter the Hermit, Walter Sans-Avoir and popular crusaders
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/1/text: Peter's followers marched from Cologne through Hungary, fought the Byzantines at Niš, were ferried across the Bosporus by Alexios and were annihilated by the Turks near Civetot in October 1096.
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/2/titl: Emicho's band and the Rhineland massacres, 1096
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/2/peop: Count Emicho of Flonheim and allied bands
conflicts/first-crusade/campaigns/2/text: Moving up the Rhine in May 1096, bands associated with Emicho attacked Jewish communities at Speyer, Worms and Mainz before being routed by the Hungarians at Moson.
